artworks.title: Medea's Gift to Creusa (Louvre CA 2193)
artworks.description: Apulian red-figure crater in the Louvre: Creusa (Glauce) receives Medea's fatal bridal gifts while the children stand by. The vase freezes Euripides' Corinthian murder — the princess who put on poisoned robes and burned.

artworks.title: Creusa Receiving the Burning Jewelry from Medea
artworks.description: Medieval illumination of Glauce/Creusa as Medea's jewels catch fire — the Corinthian bride's death staged for a manuscript audience. The Latin name Creusa stands for Creon's daughter whom Euripides called Glauce.

artworks.title: Medea, or the Marriage of Jason and Creusa
artworks.description: Rembrandt's etching for Jan Six's Medea stages the Corinthian wedding: Jason and Creusa (Glauce) before the altar while Medea's tragedy gathers offstage. National Gallery of Art, Washington.

artworks.title: Medea Sarcophagus (Berlin)
artworks.description: Roman sarcophagus in Berlin: among Medea's Corinthian crimes, the children bring poisoned wedding gifts to Creusa/Glauce. Marble narrative that fixed the princess's death beside the infanticide for later ages.

popCulture.title: Medea
popCulture.creator: Euripides
popCulture.description: Euripides' Corinthian tragedy makes Glauce the new bride whose poisoned robe and diadem kill her — and Creon who clasps her burning body.

popCulture.title: Creusa (daughter of Creon)
popCulture.description: Also called Glauce — Creon's daughter, Jason's intended, Medea's victim; Latin tradition kept the name Creusa.
